“The process of identifying objective, variables, and constraints for a given problem is known as modeling. Construction of an appropriate model is the first step — sometimes the most important step — in the optimization process.”

Nocedal and Wright (2006), p. 2. Biegler (2010), §§1.1–1.2, pp. 1–4, motivates the same components through applications. A predictive model links adjustable quantities to outcomes; constraints encode physical laws, resource limits and admissible actions. Domain expertise and stakeholder priorities determine what belongs in those expressions. A technically accurate solve can still answer an unhelpful question if the objective or feasible alternatives were chosen poorly.

Implementation tools, including AI assistants, can help with the mechanics once a model is stated. Domain knowledge, stakeholder priorities and checking the formulation remain part of the analyst’s work.

What should be believed about the model?

A battery’s control schedule is an action decision; estimating efficiency is inference; choosing an informative charge/discharge experiment is an information decision. For an application in your discipline, name the adjustable quantities, the objective and where the data come from. The same mathematical machinery can support all three roles.

children.alt: Taxonomy of optimization problems. The tree splits on continuous versus discrete variables, then on differentiable versus nondifferentiable. Both branches end in a chain of inclusions read downward from the most general class to the most specific: SDP contains SOCP contains QP contains LP on the convex side, and MINLP contains MIQP contains MILP contains IP on the mixed-integer side. A separate light green band at the bottom lists six modeling paradigms -- dynamic optimization, parameter estimation and experimental design, stochastic programming, logical models, decision support, and robust optimization -- which cut across the tree rather than forming another branch of it; robust optimization carries the same dotted grey not-covered marking the tree uses. A brace labelled conic optimization groups SDP and SOCP. Boxes are shaded and outlined three ways: our focus this semester, specialized algorithms not covered, and not covered.

children.value: Three things in this chart are worth pausing on.
Each branch ends in a chain of inclusions, read downward from the most general.

On the convex side, the arrows express representability after a suitable reformulation: second-order cones admit semidefinite representations; convex QPs with affine constraints, and convex quadratically constrained QPs, admit second-order-cone epigraph formulations; and LPs are QPs with a zero quadratic term. The QP rung in this
chain excludes nonconvex QPs. SOCP and SDP are the

programs, and this chain is where they fit: they are the natural continuation of LP and QP, not a separate kingdom. We will not cover them, but it is worth knowing the ladder exists — a surprising number of engineering problems (robust design, some control synthesis, relaxations of nonconvex QPs) turn out to be conic once written the right way.
The mixed-integer side nests the same way.

Decision science and the limits of a model optimum

means studying how models, data and analytical methods support decisions under uncertainty. This is a course working definition. Optimization is one family of analytical methods; a mathematical optimum alone does not settle the broader decision process.

Decision makers, stakeholders and the organization
Ability to use evidence and analysis in the intended decision process

Driscoll et al. (2023), pp. 148–149, describe the four-phase systems decision process as iterative and centered on decision-maker and stakeholder values. The labels are not an automatic four-step algorithm for an ill-defined situation. The older three-phase shorthand attributed to Herbert Simon,
The New Science of Management Decision
(1960), is intelligence, design and choice: understanding the problem, developing possible actions and choosing among them. The four-phase systems view makes implementation explicit.

Wong-Parodi et al. (2020) uses the coastal-planning example to examine how quantitative analysis supports deliberation about tradeoffs. The model, institutional process, evidence and stakeholder input work together. The closing
gives the explicitly labelled prose paraphrase of the review’s contribution and the historical case’s limits.
Check the framing as well as the computation

Ackoff (1979), p. 97, criticizes assessing an optimized model through the same model assumptions: managers’ real choices and the modeled optimum can differ for reasons missing from the formulation. His statement that models simplify reality occurs in that critique, not as proof that any simplified optimum is useful. Check representation and consequences independently of the solver’s internal certificate.

The familiar paired aphorism “All models are wrong, but some are useful” is attributed to George E. P. Box. The precise printed source of that paired wording remains uncertain in the course record; do not treat the held 1976 article as verification of both halves. The methodological issue is whether a model is adequate for the decision and evidence at hand.

Rittel and Webber (1973), pp. 161–162, distinguish public-planning problems with no definitive formulation, no inherent stopping rule and solutions judged good/bad rather than simply true/false. Defining alternatives, constraints and the performance measure is part of that framing work. The claim concerns these planning contexts; it does not imply that feasibility or an optimality certificate for an already specified mathematical model is a matter of opinion. Their argument also challenges prematurely treating a wicked problem as though its goals were settled.

For a battery revenue model that ignores aging, an accurately optimized high-cycle schedule can expose a missing consequence. Discuss the operating priorities and data, then add a justified degradation cost or throughput restriction. Tightening tolerances does not add an omitted cost. A model can fail through poor numerical scaling, violated algorithm assumptions, or a mismatch between the mathematical objective and the actual decision; these are different diagnoses.
